content: The internet, for example, provides access to works that are publicly available but not necessarily in the public domain. Copying such works may infringe upon the copyright held by the author. If a pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work is considered a useful article, it is only eligible for copyright protection if its aesthetic features can be separated from its functional features. A useful article is defined as an object with an inherent utilitarian function that is not solely intended to depict its appearance or convey information. For such works to be copyrighted, their aesthetic aspects must be separable from their functional aspects. There are two main approaches to determining separability: physical separability and conceptual separability. Physical separability refers to the ability to physically remove the aesthetic component from the functional component. Conceptual separability, on the other hand, can be established in various ways. For instance, it may exist if the useful article is also appreciated for its aesthetic appeal or if the design process allows the designer to make artistic choices independent of functional considerations. Another way to assess conceptual separability is to consider whether an individual can perceive the aesthetic aspects of the work as distinct from its functional aspects. Several tests are used to evaluate conceptual separability. The Primary Use Test asks whether the primary purpose of the object is artistic or functional. The Marketable as Art Test examines whether the article can be sold as art, regardless of its functionality, though this test is often criticized because nearly anything can be marketed as art. The Temporal Displacement Test considers whether the object can be conceptualized as art without simultaneously considering its functionality. Lastly, the Denicola Test evaluates the extent to which the work reflects artistic expression that is not constrained by functional considerations. If the shape or design of an object is primarily dictated by functional requirements, the artistic aspects are considered limited by those constraints. Copyright duration varies across jurisdictions and depends on factors such as the type of work (e.g., musical composition, novel), whether the work has been published, and whether it was created by an individual or a corporation. In most countries, the default copyright term is the life of the author plus either 50 or 70 years. In the United States, the term for most works is a fixed number of years after the date of creation or publication. Copyrights generally expire at the end of the calendar year in which the term concludes. The length and requirements for copyright duration are subject to legislative changes, and numerous adjustments have been made in various countries since the early 20th century. For example, the United States previously required copyrights to be renewed after 28 years to remain in effect and mandated a copyright notice upon first publication. In Italy and France, post-war extensions increased copyright terms by approximately six years in Italy and up to 14 years in France. Many countries have retroactively extended their copyright terms. International treaties establish minimum copyright terms, but individual countries may enforce longer terms. In the United States, all works published before 1923 are in the public domain. Additionally, works published before 1964 that did not have their copyrights renewed 28 years after their first publication are also in the public domain, except for works originally published outside the U.S. by non-Americans, provided they remain under copyright in their home country. If the author has been deceased for more than 70 years, the work is in the public domain in most, but not all, countries. For instance, in Spain, some works are protected for 80 years after the author's death. In 1998, the United States extended copyright terms by 20 years under the Copyright Term Extension Act, a move heavily promoted by corporations with valuable copyrights nearing expiration. This legislation has faced significant criticism. As an example, the famous work Peter Pan, or The Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up has a complex and disputed copyright history. In the United States, typeface designs are not protected by copyright, and the Copyright Office does not accept applications for their registration. However, if a typeface design is novel and non-obvious, it may qualify for protection under a design patent. For instance, U.S. Design Patent No. 289,773, issued on May 12, 1987, covered a typeface design by Charles A. Bigelow and Kris A. Holmes. In Germany, a special extension to the design patent law was passed in 1981 to protect typefaces, allowing them to be registered as designs. Similarly, the United Kingdom passed a law in 1989 making typeface designs copyrightable, with the law also applying retroactively to designs created before 1989. In several countries, including Great Britain and the United States, it is legal to produce alternative versions of copyrighted works, such as large print or Braille editions, to improve accessibility for blind and visually impaired individuals. This can be done without obtaining permission from the copyright holder.
